title: Chuck and Chuckles' lightning joke and vibraphone gag
summary: The pair keep Buck and Bubbles' lightning patter and add the vibraphone made-it-myself gag.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Well, I'd like to get into a little bit of what Chuck and Chuckles' routines were, in terms of comedy, what kind of comedy they did, and if you can recall any of those routines, like you did with Buck and Bubbles before.

Yes. Well, the Chuck and Chuckles routines consisted of the same format, telling of the jokes. Like they'd do a song and a dance and they would exit. And then one of them, which was Chuck, myself, would run back on stage until Chuckles would call him and stop him. And he would say these jokes about, 'What you running for? Looks like it's going to rain out there. I don't want to get wet. See, I've got on a rented costume.' 'It ain't you're scared of getting wet. You're afraid of lightning.' I'd say, 'Who's afraid of

lightning?" He'd say, "You are." "The other day a thunder-storm came up, the lightning flashed, and you ran down into the dark cellar and hid." I'd say, "Well, I've got to protect myself." And he'd say, "Well, protect yourself? Don't you know if lightning's going to hit you it's going to hit you?" And I'd say, "Well, if lightning's going to hit me, leave it look for me."
That's the same as with Buck and Bubbles.
Did you continue that act? In other words, you continued that from the Buck and Bubbles routine and did it as a solo?

Well, the jokes we did. We continued doing the jokes. And we added like new jokes to the continuity, like say for instance, I said Chuckles began playing the vibraphone, you see? So somewhere along in there he would walk out of the spotlight and go and bring on the instrument, vibraphone. So when I look around and see him pushing it out of the wings onto the stage, and I'd ask him, I'd say, "Say, Chuckles, what's this you've got there?" He'd say, "These is vibraphones. I made them." I'd say, "You made them?" He'd say, "Sure I did. I walked into the music store and the man wasn't looking, so I made them." And then I'd ask him, I'd say, "Well, now, Chuckles, can you play them?" He'd say, "Can

I play them?" "Did you ever hear of Lionel Hampton?" And I'd say, "Sure, I did." Then I'd say, "What's his name?" He'd say, "Who?" And I'd say, "Lionel Hampton," and he said, "Never heard of him." And then he began to play, "Lady Be Good".
